newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Yilmaz in coalition talks with president.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Yilmaz in coalition talks with president.

text.p: Turkish opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz geared up for an appointment at the presidential palace on Friday amid speculation he was to be asked to form an "Islamist-free" government after months of political turmoil.
President Suleyman Demirel invited Yilmaz to his residence for talks at 5 p.m. (1400 GMT), Anatolian news agency said. It gave no more details of the meeting, their second in two days.
Yilmaz, a staid conservative, is one of the favourites to be appointed by Demirel as prime minister-designate following the resignation of Islamist leader Necmettin Erbakan this week.
But Yilmaz's Motherland Party has only 129 deputies in the 550-seat assembly and could struggle to find enough allies from the squabbling secularist factions to win a confidence vote.
Pro-Western Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, a bitter rival, is also in the running for the top job. She has the backing on paper of 282 deputies.
Ciller, who became Turkey's first woman prime minister in 1993, is distrusted by the secularist establishment for going into coalition with the Islamists after pledging not to do so.
Aides were confident that Yilmaz would be tapped by the president. "Hope for a new start for the country has been born," party spokesman Cumhur Ersumer told a news conference.
"(The Motherland Party) is ready to take over the duties of the administration," he said.
The Istanbul stock market index, battered by recent political chaos, closed up 2.56 percent on hopes that Demirel would give Yilmaz the nod, brokers said.
Erbakan, NATO member Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, quit on Wednesday after pressure from secularist generals and rows over religious activism within his ruling alliance.
He had asked Demirel to approve a plan under which Ciller would head a new coalition with the Islamists to take Turkey to early elections.

Erbakan aides said they were not unduly worried by the news that Yilmaz had been called to the presidential palace. "Perhaps the president feels he should have further consultations," deputy chairman Oguzhan Asilturk told reporters.
"Nobody should expect anything above and beyond that. He cannot give the task to Yilmaz," Asilturk said.

Yilmaz, prime minister twice since 1991, went to Ankara's main Kocatepe mosque for Friday prayers after Demirel's invitation. A bouquet of flowers sent by a well-wisher stood outside the Yilmaz family home, witnesses said.
The leaders of two leftist parties said after a series of meetings with Demirel on Thursday that they would support conservative Yilmaz in parliament.
But the planned secularist alliance would still need backing from a small right-wing group and around a dozen defections from Ciller's True Path Party to forge a government.

Yilmaz was confident he could get past a parliamentary vote of confidence. "There is an extremely high possibility that a government formed under me can win a vote of confidence," he told the NTV television news channel late on Thursday night.
Turkish media said the president did not favour Ciller, Islamist Erbakan's ally in an "odd couple" coalition since last June.
"The president does not want to give priority to Ciller," the Hurriyet daily quoted sources close to Demirel as saying.
"If he had wanted to do that he would not have wasted Turkey's time. He would have asked her to form a new government as soon as Erbakan resigned," one unnamed source said.
Another mainstream newspaper carried similar quotes.
The president's press office said in a statement that he would meet armed forces chief General Ismail Hakki Karadayi later on Friday for what it called a regular meeting.
The army has a long history of intervention in politics, deposing three governments in the last four decades.
Top commanders have branded religious activism as "public enemy number one" and last week made a veiled threat to use force to halt the Islamists.
